doc.title: Eddie Marshall interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

chapter: Family and early playing in Springfield
title: Playing R&B with Uncle Cookie at the Horseshoe
summary: At 16 he played with Uncle Cookie's Seven Sharps at a segregated all-black Springfield club, skipping school and earning less than with his father.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: A swing and something Latin which was always [scats] — it was just terrible. I never heard or seen a Latin band, but I heard it on the radio and everything. And so I did that and then my Uncle Cookie, who had a band called the Seven Sharps, this was when I was in high school, I was 16 then, and I played with his band at a club. My mom actually let me go to this club called the Horseshoe in Springfield, Mass, and play drums with my Uncle Cookie. Now this was an R&B band. And this club, the Horseshoe, you have to realize everything was segregated back in those days you know. And so all the black folks were down on the south end. And I worked there with my uncle that first night and I was just totally gone. There was a fight, there was like everything. It was a totally all black club. And one of those types of places. It was just a hoot. You just could not believe it. And the music was just killing. Because it’s R&B and I really, really liked that. So I didn’t work for my dad anymore after that. And it went from like we were making like, I was making twenty dollars a night with my dad and eleven dollars a night with Cookie at the Horseshoe. But it was three nights in a row. And actually it ended up, by the time I left high school, four nights. And I did that for like two or three years and of course I never went to school on Friday, and I never went to school on Monday.

And I had one of the lowest grade point averages ever recorded in the school history. But by that point I was totally obsessed with music. And it was just being in that environment. And I mean playing dance music, I mean that’s what the whole thing is. It was never — I never had the mentality of being like a drum star, even though in those days my hero was Gene Krupa. Because that’s how I really started liking drums anyhow, by going to the movies and seeing the old news reels of Benny Goodman and Gene Krupa. And he just — I even got to take a lesson with him.
